prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

ATLANTA, Georgia (CNN) -- One of the best gifts you can give a child this holiday season may not be the latest gadget, toy, or tasty treat, but instead the gift of a healthy lifestyle. Participants get a workout at the FitWit fitness boot camp. An Atlanta-based non-profit organization is doing its part to combat childhood obesity by teaching kids proper nutrition and exercise in a six-week fitness boot camp similar to NBC's "The Biggest Loser." The FitWit Foundation hopes its program will catch on nationwide. "We wanted to work with teens in a meaningful way, and we saw firsthand how fitness and physical activity in general is being neglected in this population. With a lot of help from volunteers and donors, we've started a program this past spring that encourages hard work and is a fun way to get in shape," said FitWit instructor Ben Thoele. FitWit's program is a six-week after-school boot camp competition which rewards participants with prizes for meeting fitness goals. An iPod Nano was the grand prize for Atlanta Public Schools students completing a recent fitness session.  Watch for more on FitWit » . Students who are motivated to get in shape but not involved in an organized sports team are selected as contestants. Participants' fitness levels are assessed at the beginning and end of the program. Each week, volunteers lead three 60-minute sessions that include fitness instruction and physical health education. In addition, the participants are assigned two home workouts to be performed between sessions. "After six weeks, all participants have an increased total fitness ability. We averaged over 40 percent improvement in total fitness in our first program last spring. It's common to have a participant double their fitness ability," Thoele said. "A lot of these kids don't know how to work out, or that they even have the capacity to work out. They gain an appreciation for pushing their limits, and when that happens, we see a tremendous boost in their self-confidence," he said. The need for increased fitness across the country is striking. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 17.6 percent of U.S. teenagers were obese in 2006 -- more than triple the rate in 1980.  Obesity puts the teens at increased risk for heart disease, bone and joint problems, sleep apnea, and social and psychological problems, the CDC says. "Success for us is when a kid is thinking about fitness outside of the program, because they enjoy how they feel when they're in better shape," Thoele said. "Our first winner, Raquel, told us that she continued to come because she just felt better. She had incredible numbers as well. She was not able to perform even one sit-up at the start of the program and did 21 in our final assessments. She also shed more than 90 seconds off her mile time." "Since I've been here, I've been eating healthy," one FitWit participant said. "I have been watching what I eat and drink. I drink three cups of water every day. And I exercise more often. I don't spend too much time inside my home anymore."

**ATLANTA, Georgia (CNN) —** This holiday season, helping a child develop lifelong healthy habits could be more valuable than giving the newest electronic device, toy, or sweet snack.

Young people in Atlanta are exercising through FitWit, a fitness boot camp operated by a local nonprofit. The organization is working to address childhood obesity by providing children with nutrition guidance and physical training during a six-week program modeled after NBC’s *“The Biggest Loser.”* The FitWit Foundation would like to see the initiative expand throughout the United States.

FitWit instructor Ben Thoele said the organization wanted to connect with teenagers in a significant way after observing that fitness and physical activity were often overlooked among this age group. With substantial support from donors and volunteers, FitWit launched the program in the spring, creating an enjoyable but demanding way for participants to improve their physical condition.

The program is structured as a six-week, after-school competition in which students earn prizes by reaching fitness targets. In one recent session, an iPod Nano was awarded as the top prize to participating Atlanta Public Schools students. Additional information about FitWit was also available in a related video.

Contestants are chosen from students who want to become fitter but do not belong to an organized athletic team. Their physical abilities are measured both before and after the program. Volunteers conduct three one-hour sessions every week, combining exercise coaching with lessons about physical health. Participants must also complete two workouts at home between the supervised meetings.

Thoele said everyone who finishes the six weeks shows an overall improvement in fitness. During the first program in the spring, participants improved by an average of more than 40 percent, and some commonly increased their fitness capacity twofold.

Many of the children begin without knowing how to exercise or realizing what they are physically capable of doing, Thoele explained. As they learn to challenge themselves, they begin to value testing their limits and often experience a major rise in self-confidence.

National statistics demonstrate the seriousness of the problem. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported that 17.6 percent of American teenagers were obese in 2006, a proportion more than three times higher than it had been in 1980. According to the CDC, obesity increases adolescents’ chances of developing heart disease, sleep apnea, bone and joint conditions, and psychological and social difficulties.

For FitWit, Thoele said, real achievement occurs when participants continue thinking about exercise beyond the program because they like the way better fitness makes them feel.

The program’s first winner, Raquel, said she kept attending because her improved health made her feel better. Her results were also dramatic: At the initial assessment, she could not complete a single sit-up, but by the final evaluation she performed 21. She also reduced her one-mile running time by more than 90 seconds.

Another FitWit participant said the program had led to healthier eating and drinking choices. The student began paying closer attention to food and beverages, drinking three cups of water each day, exercising more regularly, and spending less time indoors at home.

counterfactuals.output:
# Atlanta nonprofit uses fitness boot camp to help teenagers build healthier habits

**ATLANTA** — For six weeks, a group of Atlanta teenagers is trading screen time for squats, sprints and lessons about healthy eating.

The fitness boot camp, organized by the nonprofit FitWit Foundation, aims to combat childhood obesity by making exercise accessible and teaching young people how nutrition affects their health.

Participants complete age-appropriate workouts designed to improve strength, endurance, coordination and confidence. Alongside the physical training, the program offers nutrition education intended to help teenagers make healthier choices at home and at school.

The approach reflects a broader effort among health organizations to address childhood obesity through sustainable lifestyle changes rather than short-term weight loss. According to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, childhood obesity can increase the risk of conditions including Type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure and heart disease.

FitWit Foundation’s program emphasizes consistency and personal progress. The boot camp format allows teenagers to work alongside peers, creating a supportive environment that can make exercise feel more social and less intimidating.

Nutrition is another key part of the initiative. Teenagers learn how food choices, portion sizes and hydration can affect energy levels and athletic performance. The goal is to give participants practical information they can continue using after the six-week program ends.

By combining exercise with education, the Atlanta nonprofit hopes to help young people develop habits that extend beyond the boot camp — and to show that fitness can be challenging, rewarding and fun.

counterfactuals.output:
*Editor’s note: The names, quotations and local results below are illustrative and should be replaced with verified reporting before publication.*

## After-school fitness challenge helps teens build healthier habits

**RIVERTON, May 15** — An after-school fitness program inspired by the television competition “The Biggest Loser” concluded this week with organizers emphasizing healthier habits, improved fitness and teamwork rather than rapid weight loss.

Twenty-four students participated in the eight-week “Fit for Life Challenge” at Riverton Community Center. The program met three afternoons a week and combined supervised exercise, nutrition lessons and weekly wellness goals. Students took part in strength training, walking, dance, relay races and noncompetitive games, while registered dietitian-led sessions covered hydration, sleep, portion awareness and preparing balanced snacks.

At the final assessment, 19 participants improved at least one fitness measure, such as cardiovascular endurance, flexibility or the number of pushups they could complete. Collectively, students increased their average six-minute walking distance by 12 percent. Fourteen reported being physically active for at least 60 minutes on five or more days during the final week, compared with seven when the program began.

Individual weights were kept confidential, and rankings were based on attendance, effort and progress across several health measures.

“We borrowed the excitement and team structure of ‘The Biggest Loser,’ but we did not want students judging success by a number on a scale,” instructor Maya Collins said. “For teenagers, the goal should be building confidence, finding activities they enjoy and developing habits they can maintain.”

Participant Jordan Lee, 15, said the program made exercise feel less intimidating.

“At first, I could barely finish the warmup without stopping,” Lee said. “By the end, I could jog the whole track loop. I also learned that being healthy isn’t about skipping meals—it’s about having enough energy to do what you want to do.”

Students earned points for attending sessions, supporting teammates, completing activity logs and meeting personal goals. The top team received donated fitness trackers, while individual awards included athletic shoes, recreation-center memberships, sports equipment and grocery-store gift cards. Every participant received a certificate and water bottle.

Program coordinator Elena Ramirez said staff were trained to avoid public weigh-ins, restrictive dieting and elimination-style competitions associated with some reality television programs.

“We wanted the motivation of a challenge without the shame,” Ramirez said. “No one was voted out, and no one was encouraged to pursue unsafe weight loss. Every student had a chance to succeed.”

Childhood obesity remains a significant public-health concern. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, about one in five U.S. children and adolescents has obesity. CDC data from 2017 through March 2020 put obesity prevalence among adolescents ages 12 to 19 at **22.2 percent**. The agency defines childhood obesity as a body mass index at or above the 95th percentile for children of the same age and sex.

The CDC recommends that children and adolescents ages 6 to 17 get at least 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity each day, including aerobic activity and regular muscle- and bone-strengthening exercise.

Organizers plan to offer the program again in the fall and are considering a family session so parents and guardians can participate in cooking demonstrations and weekend activities.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

# Give Children the Gift of a Healthy Lifestyle This Holiday Season

For many Atlanta families, the holiday season is a time for giving. FitWit is encouraging the community to consider a gift that can benefit children long after the decorations come down: the confidence, knowledge and support to live a healthy, active life.

Through its Atlanta youth fitness initiative, FitWit helps young people build positive relationships with exercise and wellness. The program makes fitness approachable through age-appropriate workouts, team activities and encouragement from coaches and peers. Rather than focusing only on athletic performance, FitWit emphasizes progress, consistency and personal growth.

That approach can be especially meaningful for children who have limited access to organized sports, safe exercise spaces or structured wellness programs. By reducing those barriers, the initiative gives more Atlanta youth opportunities to move, learn and discover what they are capable of achieving.

The benefits extend beyond physical fitness. Completing a challenging workout, learning a new skill or supporting a teammate can strengthen confidence and resilience. Participants also practice habits such as setting goals, staying accountable and persevering when something feels difficult—lessons that can carry into the classroom, relationships and future leadership roles.

FitWit’s coaches aim to create an environment where every child can participate, regardless of experience or ability. Success might mean improving strength or endurance, but it can also mean showing up consistently, trying something new or becoming more comfortable working as part of a team.

The need for this kind of support does not end with the holiday season. Healthy habits develop over time, and young people are more likely to sustain them when they have access to trusted mentors, welcoming spaces and a community that celebrates their progress.

Community support helps make those opportunities possible. Donations can assist with coaching, equipment, program access and other resources needed to deliver high-quality youth fitness experiences. Volunteers, local businesses and community partners can also contribute by sharing expertise, providing supplies or helping more families learn about the program.

This holiday season, Atlanta residents can give more than a traditional present. By supporting FitWit’s youth fitness initiative, they can help children gain tools that may serve them for years: strength, self-belief, healthy routines and a sense of belonging.

Toys are outgrown and gadgets are replaced. The gift of a healthy lifestyle can last a lifetime.

To learn more, volunteer or support FitWit’s Atlanta youth fitness initiative, visit **[insert website or donation link]**.

# Beyond the playing field: FitWit volunteers help students build healthier lives

**By CNN Health**

For students who are not involved in organized sports, opportunities to exercise can be limited. FitWit volunteers are working to close that gap by offering supportive fitness programs designed to help young people become stronger, more confident and better informed about their health.

Instead of focusing on competition or athletic ability, FitWit activities emphasize participation and personal progress. Volunteers guide students through age-appropriate workouts that may include running, body-weight exercises, relay games, stretching and team challenges. Exercises can be modified so beginners participate alongside students with more experience.

The goal is to make movement feel accessible — not intimidating.

For some students, that can mean discovering they are capable of completing a difficult workout. For others, it may be learning how to set a realistic goal, support a teammate or keep trying after a setback. Those small successes can help build confidence that carries into the classroom and other parts of life.

Volunteers also encourage students to develop healthier habits beyond each session. Discussions about nutrition may cover practical choices such as drinking more water, eating fruits and vegetables, choosing balanced meals and paying attention to how food affects energy. The emphasis is on sustainable decisions rather than restrictive dieting.

Consistency is another key lesson. Students are encouraged to view exercise as something they can incorporate into daily life, even if they do not belong to a team or have access to a gym. Walking, dancing, playing outside and completing short workouts at home can all contribute to an active routine.

FitWit’s volunteer-led approach also gives students positive adult role models. By exercising alongside participants, celebrating effort and creating a judgment-free environment, volunteers show that fitness can be social, enjoyable and open to everyone.

The program’s broader message is simple: Young people do not have to consider themselves athletes to benefit from physical activity. With encouragement and accessible instruction, students can improve their fitness, make more informed food choices and develop exercise habits that may continue long after the program ends.
